To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

* Robustness to random perturbation and adversarial robustness are naturally characterized by q=1 and q=\infin, respectively; * The robustness between these extremes can be characterized by intermediate values of q, which we call intermediate robustness;

1) the intermediate-q robustness of a model is an important metric that is not well-captured by the traditional random and worst-case metrics, and 2) the q-norms of a classifier are efficiently estimable by path sampling.

(1) a sliding scale of robustness metrics exists between robustness to random and adversarial perturbatations; (2) this sliding scale can be estimated efficiently by path sampling of the associated partition functions; and (3) this sliding scale provides insight into the tradeoffs that different robustness metrics impose on the robustness of the resulting classifier.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: How robust are deep networks to intermediate perturbations? How does robustness vary with the norm of the perturbation? How can we efficiently estimate the robustness to intermediate perturbatons?
the question: what is the most robust classifier for a given task and dataset?
the question of how well a machine learning model performs not just on its training data, but on data drawn from a different distribution.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

our paper proposes a new way to estimate robustness of machine learning classifiers to intermediate perturbations, and shows that this is a valuable additional metric to gauge robustness, which provides a clear tradeoff in robustness between classifiers that optimize data-augmentation and those that optimize adversarial training.
the proposed method is a valuable tool for measuring intermediate robustness.

the paper proposes a novel method to quantify the robustness of a given classifier, which is defined as the expected performance of the classifier under a given distribution of adversarial perturbances, and that the method is based on a Monte Carlo estimation of a partition function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we provide a novel way to quantify the robustness of a machine learning model.
we propose a new metric to evaluate robustness, and a new method to estimate this metric.

we propose a novel way to measure robustness, and show that it can be used to measure the performance of classifiers trained using different methods, and that there is a tradeoff in robustness depending on the training method.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the robustness of a given classifier can be evaluated along a spectrum of different metrics, each of which is useful for different purposes.
the robustness of a model to random perturbbations and adversarial attacks are not the only two metrics by which to gauge its robustness.

there is a natural sliding scale between robustness to random noise and robustness to worst-case noise, and this scale provides a valuable additional tool by which to measure and compare the test-time robust performance of different classifiers.
